title: Few marching bands and instruments around 1912-14
summary: He explains that marching bands and pianos were rare for black communities, and that Bunk Johnson and Eubie Blake were rarities.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Getting my first drums, with or without lessons

blocks.x: Very few marching bands. There were very few marching bands. I don't remember...well, before I left Waco, they had marching bands, but around 1912, '13, there were very few marching bands. You know, and there was this war hysteria, you know what I mean, and it was just before World War I when in 1914 you had the conflict in Europe. Very few marching bands. People marched, but they didn't march with bands. You didn't have that many/ instrumentalists let's face it. said I'd I'd like to see that...sometimes I/ like to go to Wurlitzer's and look in the archives and see how many pianos did they sell in various regions, and I'd bet it would be alarming, that you'd have very few. You know, people

start talking about who did this and who did that, but back in those days if Eubie Blake played, he was a rarity. And the piano wasn't in tune. Because they didn't have any piano tuners you know, that care, you played in just a dive, a juke joing, backwood, you know, that was the ind of thing, so you had very few instruments, and when I hear these guys talking about in Bunk Johnson did this and Bunk Johnson did that. It's possible that he did it, but he was a rare case.
But we'll get to that a little later on...
